anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statements or transaction demarcations force the engine to read, scan, or hold more data and locks than the business logic really requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, column, partition, or indexing choices do not align with access patterns, obliging otherwise correct queries to traverse large data regions or touch non-covering paths.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent sessions request mutually incompatible locks on the same rows, pages, tables, or metadata, producing long blocking chains or deadlocks that stall OLTP throughput.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits an interwoven symptom set: statements appear persistently in slow-query and deadlock logs; execution plans show table or index scans and wide lock footprints; lock-wait time, deadlock frequency, and transaction latency climb together; connection pools back up while CPU and I/O fluctuate between under-utilization during waits and sudden spikes when blocks clear; end-user requests time out or retry, and even modest workload spikes can trigger cascading stalls.

Causally, poorly written workload logic (e.g., missing predicates, oversized batches, or long user-think-time transactions) magnifies the surface area of data each statement touches, multiplying the number and duration of locks it acquires. Because the underlying schema lacks appropriate, selective, and covering indexes, these bloated statements escalate to full scans, further enlarging lock scopes (row → page → table) and prolonging critical-section hold times. The extended locks then collide with other concurrent transactions, and the lock manager becomes a bottleneck, producing wait chains and deadlocks. In turn, these waits lengthen transaction lifetimes, making long-running statements even more susceptible to being blocked and to blocking others, creating a feedback loop in which inefficient logic, poor physical design, and lock contention reinforce each other and dramatically degrade OLTP performance.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time with no network activity after which the operating system should send a TCP keepalive message to the client.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP client connection has no network activity longer than tcp_keepalives_idle on systems supporting TCP_KEEPIDLE or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Starts TCP keepalive probing for an otherwise idle client connection; together with interval and count settings this can lead to dead connection detection.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
